title: Problem Patterns
description: Reusable problem-solving templates: how to recognize them and apply them.

entries.title: Two Pointers
entries.summary: Two indices walk through an array, usually from opposite ends or at different speeds, to test pairs in linear time. It replaces an O(n^2) pair search whenever the data is sorted or monotonic.
recognize: Array is sorted (or can be sorted)
Question asks about a pair/triplet with a target sum
entries.how_it_works: Place one pointer at each end. If the pair sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if too large, move the right pointer left. Each step discards one element forever, so the scan is linear.
pitfalls: Forgetting to sort first when the input is unsorted
Moving the wrong pointer on duplicates
Off-by-one when pointers meet
tips: Sort a copy if original indices matter
Skip duplicates deliberately for unique-triplet variants
Draw the pointer movement on a tiny example first

entries.title: Sliding Window
entries.summary: Maintain a window [l, r] over an array or string, expanding right and shrinking left to keep a property. It turns O(n^2) subarray enumeration into O(n).
recognize: Longest/shortest contiguous subarray with a condition
entries.how_it_works: Grow the right edge one step at a time and add its value to the window state. While the window violates the condition, move the left edge forward and remove its value. Each index enters and leaves once.
entries.example:
def max_sum_k(a, k):
    window = sum(a[:k])
    best = window
    for r in range(k, len(a)):
        window += a[r] - a[r - k]
        best = max(best, window)
    return best
pitfalls: Using a variable window with negative numbers (breaks monotonicity)
Forgetting to remove a[l] when shrinking
Mixing up window length (r - l + 1)
tips: Fixed-k windows need only add/remove, no inner loop
Keep a helper add/remove for frequency maps
Check: does shrinking ever need to undo? If yes, window may not apply

entries.title: Prefix Sums
entries.summary: Precompute cumulative sums so any interval sum is a constant-time subtraction. The same idea gives prefix XOR, prefix counts, and 2D prefix sums.
recognize: Many range-sum queries on a static array
entries.how_it_works: Build P where P[i] is the sum of the first i elements. Sum(l..r) = P[r+1] - P[l]. For subarray-sum-K, store seen prefix values in a hashmap and look up (current - K).
pitfalls: 1-based vs 0-based indexing in P
Integer overflow in fixed-width languages (not Python)
Forgetting P[0] = 0
tips: Hashmap + prefix sums solves subarray-sum-K in O(n)
2D version: P[i][j] with inclusion-exclusion
Prefix XOR works the same way for parity queries

entries.title: Frequency Map Counting
entries.summary: Count occurrences with a hashmap to answer equality, anagram, and pairing questions in linear time. Most O(n^2) brute forces over values collapse this way.
recognize: Pairs with a given difference or sum
'How many subarrays' with a value condition
entries.how_it_works: Sweep once, incrementing counts. Either compare two maps (anagrams) or query the map for complements as you go (pairs). The map holds exactly the state brute force recomputes.
pitfalls: Double-counting pairs (divide or order the lookup)
k = 0 needs combination logic, not pair logic
Unhashable keys (lists) — convert to tuples
tips: Counter and defaultdict cut boilerplate
For fixed alphabets, a size-26 list beats a dict
Store indices instead of counts for subarray-position problems

entries.title: Fast and Slow Pointers
entries.summary: Two pointers traverse a linked list at different speeds to find the middle or detect a cycle in O(1) space. The fast pointer laps the slow one exactly when a cycle exists.
recognize: Middle of a list in one pass
entries.how_it_works: Move slow one step and fast two steps per round. If fast reaches the end, there is no cycle. If fast meets slow, there is one; resetting one pointer to the head and walking both at speed 1 finds the cycle start.
pitfalls: Null checks in the wrong order (check fast and fast.next first)
Using == instead of identity for node comparison
Forgetting the second phase to find the cycle start
tips: k-th from end: advance one pointer k steps first
Works on any iterator-like chain, not just linked lists
Test with 0, 1, and 2 node lists

entries.title: Interval Merging
entries.summary: Sort intervals by start, then sweep once merging overlaps. Scheduling, coverage, and calendar problems all reduce to this sweep.
recognize: Insert one interval into a schedule
entries.how_it_works: Sort by start time. Keep a current merged interval; if the next interval starts after it ends, flush it and start a new one, else extend the end to the max of both ends.
pitfalls: Touching intervals ([1,2],[2,3]): decide merge-or-not from the statement
Sorting by end instead of start for merging
Mutating input when the caller reuses it
tips: Room-count variant: separate sorted starts and ends, no merging needed
For 'insert interval', binary-search the position first
Half-open [s, e) intervals make overlap logic cleaner

entries.title: Binary Search on the Answer
entries.summary: When a predicate 'x is feasible' is monotonic, binary-search the smallest feasible x instead of constructing it directly. Optimization becomes decision.
recognize: Feasibility check is easy, construction is hard
entries.how_it_works: Define feasible(x): can we do it within x? It is false...false,true...true. Binary-search the boundary, keeping the invariant that lo is infeasible and hi is feasible. Return hi.
pitfalls: Predicate not actually monotonic
Wrong initial bounds (hi must be feasible)
Infinite loop from lo/hi update mistakes
tips: Prove monotonicity in one sentence before coding
Use the lo+1<hi loop shape to avoid off-by-one
Feasibility is often greedy — check pat.greedy-intervals

entries.title: Monotonic Stack
entries.summary: Keep a stack of candidates in increasing (or decreasing) order to find the next greater/smaller element for every position in linear time. Each element is pushed and popped once.
entries.how_it_works: Scan left to right, storing indices. Before pushing i, pop while the stack top violates the order — those popped elements just found their 'next greater/smaller' at i. What remains on the stack is still monotonic.
pitfalls: Strict vs non-strict comparison changes equal-element behavior
Storing values instead of indices (loses positions)
Forgetting leftover stack entries (no greater element)
tips: Circular arrays: iterate twice with modulo indexing
Histogram needs both left and right smaller boundaries
Draw the stack contents after each step while learning

entries.title: Backtracking Template
entries.summary: Build candidates step by step, abandon a partial solution as soon as it violates constraints, and undo the last choice. Pruning is what separates it from brute force.
recognize: Search space is a decision tree
entries.how_it_works: A recursive function tries each legal choice at the current position, recurses, then undoes the choice. A validity check before recursing prunes whole subtrees. Start/undo symmetry keeps state consistent.

complexity.time: Exponential in the worst case, less with pruning

entries.example:
def subsets(nums):
    ans, path = [], []
    def dfs(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            ans.append(path.copy())
            return
        dfs(i + 1)          # skip nums[i]
        path.append(nums[i])
        dfs(i + 1)          # take nums[i]
        path.pop()          # undo
    dfs(0)
    return ans
pitfalls: Forgetting to undo (shared mutable path corrupts siblings)
Copying the path too late (aliasing)
No pruning — pure brute force times out
tips: Sort input first to skip duplicates cleanly
Pass index forward to avoid re-deciding positions
Memoize overlapping states to turn it into DP

entries.title: Greedy Choice on Intervals
entries.summary: For activity selection and similar problems, always picking the interval that ends earliest is optimal. Greedy works here because of an exchange argument, not by luck.
recognize: Exchange argument is easy to state
entries.how_it_works: Sort by end time. Greedily take each interval whose start is past the last taken end. Any optimal solution can swap in the earliest-ending interval without hurting, so greedy never loses.
pitfalls: Sorting by start instead of end
Assuming greedy works without an exchange proof
> vs >= on touching intervals
tips: If the greedy choice isn't obvious, suspect DP instead
State the exchange argument in a comment
Weighted variants need DP (see pat.knapsack-dp)

entries.title: Bitmask Enumeration and DP
entries.summary: Encode subsets of up to ~20 items as integer bitmasks to enumerate or DP over all 2^n subsets. Bit operations make transitions fast and code short.
recognize: Assignment / traveling salesman on small n
entries.how_it_works: Represent a set as bits of an integer. Iterate masks from 0 to 2^n - 1, extending by one element (mask | (1 << i)). DP[mask] stores the best value for exactly that set; transitions add one element.
pitfalls: n = 21+ explodes memory (2^n states)
Forgetting the base state dp[1<<0][0]
Iterating masks in an order that reuses updated states wrongly
tips: Precompute popcounts for speed
Meet-in-the-middle extends reach to n ~= 34
Use -1/None sentinel for unreachable states

entries.title: Topological Order and Layering
entries.summary: Order tasks so every dependency comes first; the same BFS layering gives shortest paths in DAGs and detects cycles. Many 'prerequisites' problems are topo-sort in disguise.
entries.how_it_works: Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly emit nodes with indegree 0 and decrement neighbors. If fewer nodes emerge than exist, a cycle remains. Processing in this order lets DP relax edges once for DAG shortest paths.
entries.example:
from collections import deque
def topo(n, edges):
    from collections import defaultdict
    g, ind = defaultdict(list), [0] * n
    for u, v in edges:
        g[u].append(v)
        ind[v] += 1
    q = deque([i for i in range(n) if ind[i] == 0])
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in g[u]:
            ind[v] -= 1
            if ind[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else None  # None = cycle
pitfalls: Forgetting isolated nodes (indegree 0, no edges)
Assuming the order is unique
Using DFS finish order without reversing
tips: len(order) < n is your cycle test
DAG shortest path: relax edges in topo order, one pass
Lexicographically smallest order: use a heap for the queue

entries.title: Knapsack DP Family
entries.summary: Decide take-or-skip for each item with capacity as the state dimension. 0/1, unbounded, and bounded variants differ only in loop direction and bounds.
recognize: Pick items with weight limit maximizing value
entries.how_it_works: dp[w] = best value for capacity w. For 0/1, iterate items outer and capacities descending so each item is used once. Unbounded iterates capacities ascending. Answer is max over valid states, not just dp[W].
pitfalls: Ascending loop accidentally allows reuse (unbounded)
Answer at dp[W] vs max(dp): same here, not always
W up to 1e9 needs value-based DP instead
tips: Subset-sum is knapsack with value = weight
Huge W, small values: DP over total value
Reconstruct choices by storing parent pointers

entries.title: Meet in the Middle
entries.summary: Split an exponential problem into halves, enumerate each half, then combine with sorting or hashing. It turns O(2^n) into roughly O(2^(n/2)).
entries.how_it_works: Enumerate all subset sums of each half (2^(n/2) each). Sort one half; for each sum in the other, binary-search the best complement. Sorting dominates the cost.
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE closest_subset_sum(a, target):
  split a into L, R
  sums_L = all subset sums of L
  sums_R = sorted(all subset sums of R)
  best = infinity
  for s in sums_L:
    t = binary_search_largest_leq(sums_R, target - s)
    best = min(best, abs(target - (s + t)))
  return best
pitfalls: Forgetting the empty subset in enumeration
2^(n/2) memory still explodes past n ~= 46
Duplicates across halves need multiset care in counting variants
tips: Sort + binary search is the standard combiner
Also applies to Hamiltonian-ish and Horowitz-Sahni knapsack
Bitmask enumeration is the n <= 20 fallback

entries.title: Digit DP
entries.summary: Count numbers in [0, X] with a digit property by DP over the decimal string with tight/loose and started flags. Range answers are f(R) - f(L-1).
recognize: Count numbers with digit constraints in a range
entries.how_it_works: Process digits left to right with state (pos, tight, started). tight=1 means the prefix equals X so far, restricting the next digit; started tracks leading zeros. Memoize on (pos, tight, started, extra).
pitfalls: Memoizing tight=1 states (they depend on the bound)
Leading zeros counted as digits
f(L-1) with L = 0 edge case
tips: Always convert range queries to prefix differences
started flag handles the number zero correctly
Extra state (sum mod k, mask) composes the same way

entries.title: Divide and Conquer DP Optimization
entries.summary: When the optimal split point is monotone in the prefix length, compute each DP layer with divide and conquer instead of trying all splits. O(k n^2) drops to O(k n log n).
recognize: DP[i] = min over j<i of (prev[j] + cost(j+1, i))
Partition sequence into k groups problems
entries.how_it_works: Optimality monotonicity: opt[l] <= opt[l+1]. Compute dp for mid using only opt range from solved neighbors, then recurse on both halves with narrowed ranges. Each layer touches each state O(log n) times amortized to O(n).
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE compute(l, r, opt_l, opt_r):
  if l > r: return
  mid = (l + r) // 2
  find best j in [opt_l, min(mid-1, opt_r)] minimizing prev[j] + cost(j+1, mid)
  dp[mid] = that value; remember best j
  compute(l, mid-1, opt_l, best)
  compute(mid+1, r, best, opt_r)
pitfalls: Applying without proving monotonicity (wrong answers)
Cost function must be computable fast or the win evaporates
Aliasing prev/cur layers
tips: Knuth optimization is the stricter special case (O(k n))
Test monotonicity empirically on small n first
Aliens trick pairs well when k is the Lagrange parameter
